data.title: AI Power Plays Need Data Centers Built, Analyst Says. It Doesn't Matter Where. — Barrons.com
data.description:
By Mariapaula Gonzalez

A Democratic sweep of Congress this week triggered panic among investors worried that officials will block data center construction in their communities.

Among those caught in the backlash: Vertiv Holdings and other AI power plays.

But local votes shouldn't matter that much to those companies. As long as data centers get built somewhere, Bespoke Investment Group noted Friday, the location itself is irrelevant.

"With the semis down nearly 40% from their peak on 6/22, the AI trade is in a nasty bear market," the firm wrote in a note Friday.

"It's a big world out there, however," the firm added. "And there are a lot of picks and shovels stocks tied to the data center buildout that are location agnostic, as long as the data centers get built somewhere."

How many will get built — and when — is a question following the shift in control of Congress. But when data centers get built, equipment suppliers make them run with chips, cooling systems and power components.

Many of those companies could use the boost.

Optical and networking stocks have plunged roughly 45% since the June 22 peak, with power and backup equipment sliding about 43% and thermal management names falling nearly 39%. Vertiv, a prominent supplier of cooling and power hardware that could face headwind from stricter oversight, has tumbled about 54% from its 52-week high, though shares rebounded 3.9% to $183.52 on Friday.

Following the midterm election results, Vertiv Holdings stock sank about 13% to $205.55 on Wednesday.

Data centers emerged as a key issue this election cycle. While companies scramble to build them fast enough for soaring AI compute demands, local opposition to hosting them has grown. Voters reacted by passing nearly every measure aimed at curbing data-center expansion.

Paradoxically, tighter rules could work in favor of hyperscalers like Amazon, Microsoft, Alphabet, and Meta Platforms. As Barron's noted this week, Wall Street has already worried these companies have been burning through too much cash building data centers. If politicians force them to slow down, that spending could slow as well, improving their cash flow and profits.

Bloom Energy was another stock poised to buck the trend. The company uses fuel cell-based on-site power to bypass the power grid, which CEO KR Sridhar previously noted could benefit from data center backlash. Shares of Bloom Energy rose 4.3% on Friday.

Write to Mariapaula Gonzalez at mariapaula.gonzalez@barrons.com

data.title: Steadright Closes Second And Final Tranche Of Financing For A Closing Total Of $900K
data.description:
(TheNewswire)

November 6th, 2026 – Muskoka, Ontario – TheNewswire - Steadright Critical Minerals Inc. (“Steadright” or the “Company”) announces the closing of the 2st and final tranche of their non-brokered private placement for gross proceeds of $370,000 CAN (the “2nd Tranche”) at a price of $0.10 cents per Unit.

The closing of the first tranche of the non-brokered private placement took place on October 28th for gross proceeds of $530,000 (the “1st Tranche”). Taken together, the two tranches totalled $900,000(the “Offering”).

Insiders participated in the 1st Tranche, subscribing for 1,100,000 units at a price of $0.10 per unit. Insiders also participated in the 2nd Tranche, subscribing for 500,000 units.

The issuance of 9,000,000 units (each, a “Unit”) in the capital of the Company consists of one common share and one common share purchase warrant (each warrant, “Warrant”) which will entitle the holder therof to purchase one common share at a price of $0.16 per common share for a period of twenty-four (24) months following the closing date.

The proceeds from the Offering will be used for general working capital, corporate purposes and potential strategic initiatives.

Securities issued to Canadians in connection with the 2nd Tranche will be subject to a statutory hold period of four (4) months and one (1) day from the date of issuance in accordance with applicable securities legislation. The remaining Units sold under in the 2nd Tranche were issued to purchasers outside of Canada pursuant to an exemption from the prospectus requirements in Canada available under OSC Rule 72-503 and, accordingly, such Units issued to purchasers outside of Canada are not subject to a four-month hold period in Canada

The 2nd Tranche remains subject to regulatory approvals, including approval from the Canadian Securities Exchange, as applicable.

The Company has paid finders’ fees to eligible parties in connection with the Offering in accordance with applicable securities laws and the policies of the Canadian Securities Exchange. Finder’s fees of $18,600 were paid on 3,100,000 of the Units, as well as well as a Finder’s Fee Warrant equal to 6% of the gross proceeds. Each Finder’s Fee Warrant will be exercisable to purchase one additional common share (the Finder’s Warrant Shares”) at $0.16 per share for a period of 24 months from closing.

ABOUT STEADRIGHT CRITICAL MINERALS INC.

Steadright Critical Minerals Inc. is a mineral exploration company established in 2019. Steadright has focussed on finding exploration and historical mining projects within the Moroccan critical mineral space. Steadright currently has exposure through a Moroccan entity known as NSM Capital Sarl, with over 192 sq. km of mineral exploration claims called the TitanBeach Titanium Project, along with the Copper Valley Project. data.title: Zevia (ZVIA) stock trades up, here is why
data.description:
What happened?

Shares of beverage company Zevia jumped 9.8% in the afternoon session after investors continued to bid up the company on its raised 2026 sales and earnings guidance from third-quarter results. The updated guidance indicated that the beverage business could reach breakeven adjusted EBITDA for the full year. Adjusted EBITDA, or earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization, is a financial measure that evaluates core operating performance by excluding interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization expenses. Zevia indicated that the potential to reach breakeven adjusted EBITDA was driven by reduced cost forecasts for aluminum and fuel.

What is the market telling us

Zevia’s shares are extremely volatile and have had 37 moves greater than 5% over the last year. In that context, today’s move indicates the market considers this news meaningful but not something that would fundamentally change its perception of the business.

The previous big move we wrote about was 1 day ago when the stock gained 5.7% on the news that the company reported an 18.4% year-over-year increase in third-quarter net sales and raised its full-year financial outlook. According to a company press release, Zevia reported third-quarter net sales of $48.34 million, up 18.4% year over year, with a gross profit margin of 46.4%. Net sales exceeded analysts' expectations of $44.98 million by 7.5%. Zevia posted a net loss of $2.2 million, or $0.03 per share, alongside an adjusted EBITDA loss of $890,000, and raised its full-year 2026 outlook for net sales and adjusted EBITDA. The per-share loss narrowed from negative $0.04 in the prior-year period and came in $0.02 ahead of consensus estimates. Additionally, free cash flow improved to $1.35 million from negative $65,000 in the same quarter last year. The combination of double-digit top-line growth and upgraded full-year guidance appeared to bolster investor confidence.

Zevia is down 26.1% since the beginning of the year, and at $1.49 per share, it is trading 45.2% below its 52-week high of $2.71 from November 2025. Investors who bought $1,000 worth of Zevia’s shares 5 years ago would now be looking at only $123.24.

ALSO WORTH WATCHING: Nvidia’s Quiet Partner. Nvidia’s chips cost a hundred grand. The connectors that make them work cost even more. One company makes them all.

Every AI server needs specialized infrastructure the chip companies don’t make. High-speed cables. Power connectors. Thermal sensors. This 90-year-old company built a monopoly on it. The AI boom just started. This stock is still flying under the radar.

data.title: Treasury Yields Rise on Jobs Number, Fall for the Week — Market Talk
data.description:
1547 ET - Treasury yields rise for the day but end the week lower as markets adjust to a new political landscape while U.S. indicators remain robust. Job creation picks up in October and unemployment decreases, while inflation is expected to remain well above target in CPI data due Tuesday. The jobs data buoys yields and the dollar. Oil prices stay below $100 amid expectations that the Democrats' midterm win could apply pressure for a swift end to the war in Iran. The 10-year falls 0.069 percentage point this week, to 4.858%, down for five consecutive weeks. The two-year sheds 0.059 point to 4.520% in its sixth straight weekly decline. (paulo.trevisani@wsj.com; @ptrevisani)

1455 ET - Canadian fiscal and monetary policies could be working at cross purposes, the chief economist at BMO Capital Markets tells clients in his week-ending note. Douglas Porter says the annual Canadian government budget plan is "meatier" than expected and delivers a significant dollop of fiscal stimulus — so much so that BMO has upgraded its Canada GDP growth forecast in 2027 to 2% from 1.8%. Meanwhile, the Bank of Canada raised rates to deal with an elevated inflation forecast, and could hike again. "If that's not rowing in different directions, it's not at all obvious what would count as policy friction," Porter says. In addition, he adds, weak jobs data, a pullback in oil prices and the tech selloff could prompt BOC policymakers to reconsider whether another hike in December is required. (paul.vieira@wsj.com; @paulvieira)

1341 ET - Inflation in the U.S. is likely to moderate in data due next week, but still keep the Fed on track to hike in December, Natixis' Christopher Hodge writes. He forecasts CPI will rise about 0.29% on the month, with core at 0.22%. That would be a slowdown from September's 0.6% and 0.3% respective increases. The slowdown "will stem from a reversion of shelter prices, primarily owners' equivalent rents and lodging away from home," he says. "Similarly, the stabilization in diesel prices should help to quell price pressures in energy-intensive goods." Hodge notes the 12-month index won't be published because of last year's government shutdown. (paulo.trevisani@wsj.com; @ptrevisani)

1336 ET - Widespread Democratic victories in the midterms, particularly in the Texas and Ohio gubernatorial races, aren't likely to impact AI data centers currently under and slated for construction in 2027, Morgan Stanley analysts say. The election may put future projects at risk, they say, estimating that around 4.9 gigawatts of data center capacity are exposed in 2028. The see a total of about 12 gigawatts of capacity slated for completion by 2030 as now at risk. "Ultimately we believe that governors will put in place a set of requirements that new data center projects must meet which may delay, rather than reduce, data center volumes," the analysts say. (elias.schisgall@wsj.com)

1331 ET - The number of rigs drilling for oil in the U.S. edged up by one this week to 463, or 49 more than a year ago, oil services company Baker Hughes reports. U.S. operators have stepped up drilling since the U.S.-Iran conflict pushed up oil prices, and have raised crude oil production to a record 14 million barrels a day. At the start of the conflict, there were 407 oil rigs active in the U.S. Natural gas rigs increased by one this week to 131, and were up by three from a year ago. (anthony.harrup@wsj.com)

1317 ET - Roger Lynch's public debut as Mattel's chief executive highlighted what JPMorgan analysts see as his vision for the company's turnaround. "Indeed, his first priority is to 'strengthen the brands and win in toys,' highlighting the long-duration success of Hot Wheels as the guide path for fixing Barbie," the analysts say in a research note. "Drive innovation, his second priority, strongly relates to the first, with capital discipline the final pillar." Noticeably, Lynch's vision for the toy company doesn't seem to include the Disney-eque ambitions of his predecessor, Ynon Kreiz, they add. Under Kreiz's leadership, Mattel spent years trying to transform into a toy and entertainment company, partnering with movie studios to bring its brands to the big screen while also expanding into digital games and live experiences. (connor.hart@wsj.com)

1314 ET - Canada's annual budget plan is an ambitious effort to jumpstart business investment in the country, say Desjardins Group's chief economist Jimmy Jean and deputy chief Randall Bartlett. The economists, however, have some trepidation about the limited fiscal wiggle room that Ottawa now has. Jean and Bartlett say a continued climb in bond yields, further friction in U.S.-Canada trade and the risk of an external economic shock "could put Canada's debt-to-GDP ratio on an unsustainable path." The firm's economists add there is a sharp rise in nonbudgetary transactions, more than C$100 billion in 2028 and 2029. As a result, Jean and Bartlett estimate that public-debt charges are set to rise 42% between FY26-27 and FY30-31.(paul.vieira@wsj.com, @paulvieira)

1250 ET - Inflation in Mexico likely picked up pace in October, led by increases in noncore prices including a seasonal rise in electricity rates. The consumer price index is expected to have risen 0.55% during the month, pushing the annual rate up to 3.65% from 3.45% in September, according to analysts surveyed by The Wall Street Journal. Core CPI, which strips out energy and perishable food prices, is expected to have risen 0.32% with the 12-month rate inching up to 3.78% from 3.75% in September. Statistics institute Inegi is scheduled to report October inflation on Monday. (anthony.harrup@wsj.com)

1249 ET - The jobs report came in hotter than expected thanks in part to more manufacturing jobs linked to the AI buildout. Yet that same report could ultimately be a problem for the tech sector as it deals with one of its biggest bloodbaths in history, Coin Bureau's Nic Puckrin says in a note. A strong labor market paves the way for rates to rise again next month and remain high for longer, the analyst says. That's bad news for tech valuations and the debt-fuelled AI buildout, particularly with the specter of stricter policies coming from the new Democratic Congress, Puckrin says. (dean.seal@wsj.com)

1132 ET - A weak spot in the otherwise upbeat October jobs report was the increase in the underemployment rate, Fifth Third Commercial Bank's Bill Adams says in a note. Most of last month's increase in employment in the household survey went into part-time work, the economist says. Things looked good otherwise: employment figures for the past three months were better than expected and earnings growth was slightly better than anticipated, though it likely still lagged the October inflation figures that are due out later this month, Adams says. "On the whole, the economy is registering healthy job growth and low unemployment, albeit unevenly distributed across industries and occupations," he says. (dean.seal@wsj.com)

1112 ET - The projection for budget deficits in Canada might not give a fulsome picture of the state of the country's public finances, says TD Bank's economics team. TD Bank says that not all the spending related to large capital projects and defense equipment will show up on books due to accounting rules. Nevertheless, "interest must be paid on the debt that is borrowed," the firm says, and that will cause public-debt charges to rise more than the deficit projects. TD Bank adds the divergence between annual borrowing requirements and the deficit figure could remain wide based on the Liberal government's ambitious capital plan — aimed at upgrading and adding trade corridors and resource projects to build resilience and reduce dependence on US trade for growth. (paul.vieira@wsj.com, @paulvieira)

1102 ET - The U.K. is expected to receive increased capital inflows following more resilient economic growth and increased mergers and acquisitions, UBS strategists say in a note. In 2026, U.K. growth and productivity outperformed expectations and inbound M&A activity was strong, they say. Sterling falls 0.7% to $1.3360 versus a stronger dollar while the euro trades flat at 0.8340 pounds. The strategists have a target for the euro of 0.8350 for year-end and 0.8200 for the end of the second quarter of 2027. (miriam.mukuru@wsj.com)
